title: Saudi Arabia Downs Houthi Missiles as Regional Officials Meet in Tehran
dek: Saudi air defenses intercepted Houthi ballistic missiles and drones over Riyadh and the Eastern Province on Monday, the same day Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials opened talks with Iran aimed at preventing renewed escalation.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.alt: Skyline of Tehran, Iran, seen from Book Garden at sunset with clouds over the city

keyPoints: Saudi authorities said air defenses destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Iran-backed Houthi rebels after explosions were heard over Riyadh, and the coalition said it also downed drones.
Officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan met Iranian counterparts in Tehran, and the four countries agreed in a joint statement to continue dialogue.
The Houthis seized strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast last month, and an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh this month killed at least 13 people.
The Houthis had not commented on the latest interceptions when the reports were filed.
Al Jazeera reports Houthi forces claimed six attacks on airports and oil facilities across Saudi Arabia, despite a rare high-level meeting of Saudi and Iranian officials.
body:
Saudi Arabia said its air defenses intercepted Houthi missiles and drones on Monday, as explosions were heard over Riyadh and alerts were issued in the Eastern Province and the Al Kharj governorate. The attacks came as senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran in an effort to lower tensions in the region.

## The interceptions

Saudi authorities said they destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen, according to the Associated Press. The Saudi-led coalition later said it had intercepted three ballistic missiles and four drones launched by the Houthis, Al Jazeera reported. The coalition also reported the interception and destruction of three additional drones over the Riyadh and southern regions on Monday evening.

Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence agency issued emergency alerts in the Eastern Province and the Al Kharj governorate before the interceptions, and lifted them afterward. The agency urged residents to avoid crowds and to call 911 in an emergency. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis, the AP reported.

## The Tehran meetings

The AP reported that Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, a brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, travelled to Tehran along with Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkiye's intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin. Iranian state media published pictures of President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, attending the sessions.

Saudi Arabia said the visit was meant to open negotiating channels to "prevent the return of military escalation," according to the AP. In a joint statement issued late Monday, the four countries "agreed to continue the dialogue to strengthen cooperation amongst the four regional countries, including for peace and security in the region," Iranian state media reported.

## Why the talks matter

The regional conflict began when the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran in February, according to the AP. Pakistan and Qatar led mediation between Washington and Tehran that produced an interim peace agreement in June, but fighting between Iran and the United States resumed soon after. Conflict then flared between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia, opening a new front and deepening a humanitarian crisis in Yemen.

The Houthis seized strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed government forces in a lightning offensive last month, prompting a counteroffensive. Saudi Arabia has since stepped up its strikes on the group, the AP reported. The Houthis have also struck Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities. An attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh earlier this month killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest attack on the kingdom in the conflict, according to the AP.

The Tehran talks are a notable step, but they have not yet produced a ceasefire or a stated deal on the Houthi front. Meridian will update this story if the four countries announce a follow-up meeting or if the Houthis respond publicly.

## Houthi claims continue (Oct. 30)

Al Jazeera reported on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi forces had claimed a total of six attacks on airports and oil facilities across Saudi Arabia, despite a rare high-level meeting of Saudi and Iranian officials. The Economist reported on Oct. 29 that Saudi Arabia wants Iran to call off the Houthis and reach a deal with the United States. Casualty figures and damage assessments were not included in the reports reviewed for this update.
